title: UK to require melt and pour declarations on steel imports as Europe tightens trade rules
intro: Trade policy leads today's edition. EUROMETAL reports that the UK will require importers to declare the melt and pour country of steel imports. SGGP English Edition reports that the EU has set a tariff on certain Vietnamese cold-rolled flat products. Elsewhere in Europe, Металлургпром reports output cuts driven by high energy costs, and the South Wales Argus records anxiety among Tata Steel workers in Newport. In the United States, Nikkei Asia reports that the USW has announced a tentative labour pact with U.S. Steel. Stock Titan reports that POSCO Holdings is reviewing an iron project at Port Hedland. Much of today's material consists of headlines or brief excerpts. Where details are missing, we say so rather than fill the gaps.

analysis: Analysis: Today's material points to a common theme of steel markets organised more tightly around origin and region. A UK melt and pour declaration requirement, if implemented as reported by EUROMETAL, could strengthen enforcement of trade measures by tracing where steel is first produced rather than where it was last processed. The EU's reported tariff on Vietnamese cold-rolled products and Fastmarkets' account of Canada diverging from US markets fit the same pattern, although the excerpts give no rates or mechanisms. Meanwhile, European producers face a cost squeeze. Output cuts tied to energy prices, the reported worker anxiety in Newport and Il Foglio's description of Taranto as bereft of steel all suggest strain on the region's capacity base. On decarbonisation, gas-based DRI appears exposed to fuel security, as Iran's reported winter gas deficit illustrates. That could reinforce interest in iron supply near ore sources, which POSCO's Port Hedland review may reflect. Calls for CBAM clarity suggest that policy uncertainty, as well as cost, may be holding back investment. None of this is confirmed by the excerpts.
